title: Denarius of Tiberius (the 'tribute penny')
summary: A silver coin about 19 mm across and 1.5 mm thick, weighing roughly 3.8–3.9 g. Obverse: laureate head of Tiberius with TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS; reverse: a seated female figure (Livia as Pax) with PONTIF MAXIM. The relief here is schematic — the proportions are what the model is for; see the photograph on the Insights card for the real portrait.

title: Alabastron — the perfume flask
summary: A calcite flask of the classic shape: rounded base (it was stood in a ring or held), narrow neck, and a flat disc lip for wiping the last drop across the skin. Mark says the woman 'broke' it — snapping the sealed neck. The height modelled here (18 cm) is a typical size; the Gospels give no dimensions, and a Roman pound of nard (John 12:3) would need a flask towards the larger end of the range.

title: Tyrian shekel (tetradrachm) — the temple's silver
summary: The coin the temple tax had to be paid in: about 26 mm across, 3 mm thick, 14 g of high-grade silver — four times a denarius. Obverse: head of the god Melqart-Heracles; reverse: an eagle with the legend ΤΥΡΟΥ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΣΥΛΟΥ, 'of Tyre, holy and inviolable'. The stater in the fish's mouth (Matthew 17:27) was one of these; Judas's thirty pieces may have been.

title: Ark of the covenant — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play Exodus 25:10–22 (the instructions) or 37:1–9 (Bezalel making it) and the ark builds up verse by verse: the acacia chest, its gold overlay and molding, the rings, the poles, the Testimony, the mercy seat, and the cherubim with their wings. Elsewhere it is shown whole. The text gives only the chest (2½ × 1½ × 1½ cubits) and the cover (2½ × 1½); the metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm. Everything else, from the cover's thickness to the look of the cherubim, is reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model.

omits.ark-tablets: Bezalel's account makes the ark but does not put the Testimony in; Moses does that at Exod 40:20

estimates.ark-moulding: the text says a molding goes 'around it' but not where; it is placed at the top edge, where it would frame the cover
estimates.ark-rings: 'its four feet' (BSB) puts the rings low; the Hebrew pa'am can also mean 'corner', so some reconstructions set them higher. Ring size is not given
estimates.ark-poles: pole length and thickness are not given; modelled at ≈4½ cubits so they stand out at both ends
estimates.ark-tablets: the Testimony is the two stone tablets (Exod 31:18); their size is not given, so they are sized to lie inside
estimates.ark-mercy-seat: length and width are in the text; the thickness of one handbreadth (⅙ cubit) is the Talmud's inference, b. Sukkah 5a
estimates.ark-cherubim: the text gives no form, height or posture for the cherubim; these are schematic figures, leaning in to face each other (Exod 25:20)
estimates.ark-wings: the wings 'spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat'; their size and shape are not given, so the tips are drawn nearly meeting over the centre

sources.note: the instructions: chest and cover dimensions, overlay, molding, rings, poles, Testimony, cherubim

title: The tabernacle and its courtyard — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play through the tabernacle chapters and it goes up as they describe it. There are three accounts: the instructions (Exodus 25–30, furniture first, then the tent, then the court), Bezalel's making of it (36–38, tent first), and Moses setting it up (40:17–33, from the bases upward). In chapters 28–29, on the priests, it stays as far as the instructions have got. Everywhere else it is shown whole. The text gives the court (100 × 50 cubits, hangings 5 high), the frames (10 × 1½), the curtains and most furniture sizes, and the model follows those. Where the tent stands in the court, how thick the frames were, the outer coverings, the basin and the pattern of the weaving are all reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole tent or cut it open to see the furniture.

steps.basis: placed in the Most Holy Place, where 26:33-34 puts it
placed on the north side of the Holy Place (26:35)
placed on the south side, opposite the table (26:35)
its size (1 × 1 × 2 cubits) is in v. 2; placed before the veil (30:6)
placed between the tent and the altar, as the verse says

omits.table-bread: Bezalel's workshop makes the table but not the bread, which Moses sets out at Exod 40:23

steps.basis: the linen curtains are 'the tabernacle itself' (26:1), so they go up with the frames; the goat hair is the tent put over it in v. 19

estimates.ark: shown whole; the Ark of the covenant card builds it verse by verse and says what each of its reconstructed details rests on
estimates.table-body: 2 × 1 × 1½ cubits of acacia (25:23); the thickness of top and legs is not given
estimates.table-rim: the rim (misgeret), a handbreadth wide, is drawn as a frame joining the legs just under the top; it is also read as a border standing up round the top
estimates.table-rings: at the four corners, on the legs, just below the rim (25:26-27); ring size not given
estimates.table-vessels: plates, dishes, pitchers and bowls, of no stated size or number. Two plates hold the rows of bread, two dishes the frankincense laid on them (Lev 24:7), and a pitcher and bowl stand at each end
estimates.table-bread: twelve loaves in two rows or stacks of six (Lev 24:5-6); the loaf size is not given
estimates.lampstand-shaft: the text gives no height or layout. The 18 handbreadths (3 cubits) and the spacing of every cup, knob and flower follow b. Menachot 28b. The shapes are schematic
estimates.lampstand-branches: each pair leaves the shaft at a knob and rises to the full height (b. Menachot 28b). Curved branches follow the Arch of Titus relief of the Second Temple lampstand; Maimonides drew them straight
estimates.lampstand-branch-cups: three almond-blossom cups, a bud (knob) and a petal (flower) on each branch; where along the branch is not given, so they are set just below the lamp
estimates.lampstand-shaft-cups: four cups on the shaft: one low down, 5–6 handbreadths up, and three at the top, as b. Menachot 28b places them
estimates.lampstand-lamps: the lamps' shape is not given; small oil lamps are drawn, spouts turned north toward the table so they 'illuminate the area in front of it' (25:37)
estimates.lampstand-tools: wick trimmers and trays of no stated size, set down beside the base
estimates.linen: ten curtains of 28 × 4 make a cover 40 long and 28 across, so it hangs 9 cubits down each side and 10 down the back. The colours are in the text; the banded pattern is not, and the woven cherubim are not drawn
estimates.goat-hair: eleven curtains of 30 × 4, reaching the ground on each side (26:13); the sixth is folded double over the front (26:9)
estimates.ram-skins: no size is given; drawn over the roof and down the sides
estimates.leather: no size is given; drawn over the roof only. The animal behind 'fine leather' (tachash) is disputed
estimates.frames-south: frames are 10 × 1½ cubits (26:16); their thickness is not given, and ½ cubit is assumed for every wall
estimates.bases-south: two silver bases per frame (26:19); their size is not given
estimates.frames-west: six frames plus two corner frames (26:22-23); how the corners were joined is disputed, so the eight are drawn spread evenly across the back wall
estimates.bars: five bars a wall (26:26-27). The middle bar runs end to end through the frames (26:28) but is drawn on the outside so it can be seen; the other four are assumed to be half-length
estimates.veil: hung from the clasps (26:33). Five curtains of 4 cubits come to 20 cubits, which leaves a Most Holy Place 10 cubits square. That is derived from the curtain sizes, not stated
estimates.altar-body: 5 × 5 × 3 cubits of acacia, hollow, made of boards (27:8), so it is drawn open at top and bottom. The text does not say where in the court it stood; it is placed in the eastern half, between the basin and the gate
estimates.altar-horns: the horns' shape and size are not given
estimates.altar-utensils: pots, shovels, sprinkling bowls, meat forks and firepans (27:3), one of each, of no stated size
estimates.altar-grate: the text does not say whether the grate was inside or outside. Its corner rings carry the poles, so it is drawn outside, round the lower half (27:5)
estimates.altar-ledge: karkov, 'ledge', is a rare word whose form is uncertain; drawn as a band round the altar where the grate ends
estimates.court-south: posts drawn every 5 cubits with the corner posts shared. That makes 59, one short of the text's sixty (27:10-16), which does not say how corners were counted
estimates.gate: 20 cubits on four posts; the text gives no pattern for the embroidery
estimates.incense-altar-horns: the horns' shape and size are not given
estimates.incense-altar-rings: 'two gold rings… on opposite sides' is drawn as one ring a side; the Hebrew can also be read as two on each side
estimates.basin: no size or shape is given (30:18, 38:8)

title: Noah's ark — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play Genesis 6:14–16 and the ark builds up as God describes it to Noah: the gopher-wood hull, its rooms and its coat of pitch, then the roof, the door in the side and the three decks. Elsewhere it is shown whole. The text gives the size (300 × 50 × 30 cubits), and the model follows it. The metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm; the Ark Encounter's full-size replica in Kentucky uses a longer royal cubit of 51.8 cm, which makes it ≈155 m long. The hull's volume, 450,000 cubic cubits (≈40,000 m³ on the common cubit), is worked out from those figures, not stated. The shape, the rooms, the deck heights and the door are reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole hull or cut it open to see the decks.

steps.basis: the size in v. 15 is already built into the hull at v. 14

estimates.hull: tevah means 'a box' (the same word is used for the basket of Moses, Exod 2:3), and the text gives only length, width and height, so it is drawn as a rectangular barge. Tim Lovett's design for Answers in Genesis, whose Ark Encounter is a full-size replica, gives it a ship's hull instead, with a wind-catching bow and a skeg at the stern for seaworthiness; the text supports neither over the other. Wall thickness is not given; ½ cubit is assumed
estimates.pitch: kopher is a coating, usually taken as bitumen; drawn as a dark skin over the hull inside and out
estimates.rooms: qinnim, literally 'nests'; their number, size and layout are not given. Drawn as a room every 15 cubits either side of a 10-cubit central aisle, the partitions running through all three decks
estimates.roof: the BSB reads tsohar as 'roof' and has the walls finished a cubit below it, so the roof is drawn on posts leaving a cubit-high opening all round. Others read tsohar as 'light' or 'window': Rashi gives both a window and a sloping roof narrowing to a cubit at the top, and Lovett's design has a skylight down the middle of the roof, a 'noon light' that 'ends a cubit upward and above'. Drawn in bare wood; whether it was pitched is not said
estimates.door: 'in the side', with no size or deck given; drawn 6 × 8 cubits, midway along the lower deck
estimates.decks: three decks, the lowest being the hull floor; their heights are not given, so they are drawn equal, 10 cubits each. Rashi, after b. Sanhedrin 108b, puts people on the top deck, animals in the middle and refuse at the bottom

sources.note: the instructions: gopher wood, rooms, pitch, 300 × 50 × 30 cubits, roof, door and three decks
Noah opens 'the window he had made in the ark' (challon, a different word from the tsohar of 6:16)

title: Solomon's temple — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play 1 Kings 6–8 or 2 Chronicles 3–5 and the temple goes up as each account describes it. Kings builds the house first: walls, porch, windows, side chambers, roof, cedar panelling, gold, cherubim and doors. Then come Huram's bronzes (the pillars, the Sea and the stands), then the gold furnishings, and last the ark. Chronicles is shorter. It leaves out the side chambers and windows, and it adds a veil and the great bronze altar. Kings names one golden table, Chronicles ten; the model has ten, and in Kings only one appears. Elsewhere the temple is shown whole. The text gives the house (60 × 20 × 30 cubits), the porch, the three storeys of side chambers (5, 6 and 7 cubits wide), the inner sanctuary (a 20-cubit cube), the cherubim, the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the altar, and the model follows those. The metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm. Chronicles measures 'according to the old standard' (2 Chr 3:3), which is often taken to be the longer royal cubit of ≈52 cm; on that cubit the house would be ≈31 m long. Wall thicknesses, doorways, the court and most placements are reconstructed. Each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. The carvings of gourds, flowers, palms and cherubim, the lions and oxen on the stands and the smaller vessels are not drawn. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole house or cut it open to see the furniture. The temple also changes after it is built. Ahaz moves the bronze altar, strips the stands and sets the Sea down on stone; Hezekiah strips the gold from the doors; the Babylonians break up the bronzes, carry off the furnishings and burn the house. Read or play those passages and the temple changes verse by verse as they tell it; anywhere else, the buttons under the model show it as it was after each.
dimensions: House 60 × 20 × 30 cubits (≈ 27 × 9 × 13 m) · with porch and side chambers ≈ 92 × 52 cubits

omits.veil: Kings gives the inner sanctuary olive-wood doors (6:31-32) and no veil; the veil is in 2 Chr 3:14
omits.bronze-altar: Kings does not describe making the bronze altar; it appears only in use (8:64, 9:25), and its size comes from 2 Chr 4:1
omits.more-tables: Kings names one golden table (7:48); Chronicles has ten (2 Chr 4:8)
omits.more-bread: Kings names one golden table (7:48), so only its bread is set out

steps.basis: 'the altar of cedar' is the incense altar, 'the altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary' (v. 22); it is placed before the sanctuary's door

omits.windows: Chronicles does not mention the windows of 1 Kgs 6:4
omits.side-chambers: Chronicles does not describe the side chambers of 1 Kgs 6:5-10
omits.side-floors: Chronicles does not describe the side chambers of 1 Kgs 6:5-10
omits.stairs: Chronicles does not describe the side chambers of 1 Kgs 6:5-10
omits.floor: Chronicles does not mention the cypress floor of 1 Kgs 6:15
omits.floor-gold: Chronicles does not mention the gold floor of 1 Kgs 6:30
omits.chains: the gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary (1 Kgs 6:21) have no counterpart; Chronicles' chains are ornament on the walls (3:5) and on the pillars (3:16)

steps.basis: Chronicles gives only the length and width; the height of 30 cubits is from 1 Kgs 6:2
the beams it overlays are the roof beams of 1 Kgs 6:9, so the roof goes on here
the stands the basins rest on are only named in the list at 4:14; their form is from 1 Kgs 7:27-37

states.label: Ahaz (≈ 732 BC)
states.basis: after meeting Tiglath-pileser at Damascus, Ahaz has Uriah build an altar copied from one he saw there and moves the bronze altar to its north (16:10-14). He cuts off the stands' panels, takes down their basins, and sets the Sea down from the oxen onto a stone base (16:17). The date is Damascus's fall to Assyria, which the Assyrian records put in 732 BC. The oxen are not mentioned again, so they are taken away here. 2 Chr 28:24 adds that he cut up the temple's vessels and shut its doors, which the model does not show

states.label: Hezekiah (701 BC)
states.basis: in his fourteenth year, when Sennacherib invaded (701 BC by the Assyrian annals), Hezekiah strips the gold from the temple's doors and doorposts to pay the tribute (18:16). The text says it was gold 'he had plated', perhaps when he repaired the doors (2 Chr 29:3). Ahaz's changes are still in place; Hezekiah's reforms (2 Kgs 18:4, 2 Chr 29) do not say he undid them

states.label: Babylon (587/586 BC)
states.basis: Nebuzaradan burns the house (2 Kgs 25:9). The Chaldeans break up the pillars, the stands and the Sea and carry the bronze to Babylon, with the vessels of bronze, gold and silver (25:13-17; Jer 52:17-23), 'everything… both large and small' (2 Chr 36:18). What burned or was taken is removed in the order each account gives it. The wood and gold of the house go with the fire. The bronze altar goes with 'all the articles of bronze', which do not name it. The stone walls, the side chambers, the court and Ahaz's stone altar are left standing, because the text does not say they were torn down and it does not say how much of them survived the fire. The ark's fate is not recorded in Kings or Chronicles; it is not seen again, so it is drawn going with the house

estimates.walls: the text gives the interior (60 × 20 × 30) but not the walls' thickness. They are drawn 6 cubits thick, the figure Ezekiel's temple gives (Ezek 41:5), stepping in a cubit at each storey of the side chambers so their beams rest on the ledges (6:6). The main doorway is drawn 10 cubits wide, as Ezekiel's is (41:2), and 15 high, which is not given
estimates.portico: 20 across and 10 deep (1 Kgs 6:3). Its height is 20 in the BSB of 2 Chr 3:4, following some Greek and Syriac manuscripts; the Hebrew text reads 120. It is drawn open to the east
estimates.windows: 'narrow windows framed high' (6:4). The Hebrew is often read as windows narrowing inward, or latticed. Their number and size are not given; slots are drawn every 5 cubits above the side chambers
estimates.side-chambers: the widths of the three storeys (5, 6 and 7) and their height (5 each) are in the text (6:6, 10). The outer wall's 5 cubits follow Ezek 41:9, and the floors are assumed to be a cubit thick. The individual rooms are not drawn. The 'Ain Dara temple in Syria has a similar corridor of rooms round three sides
estimates.stairs: the Hebrew lulim is read as a winding stair or as trapdoors. Drawn as a spiral just inside the south door, whose size and place along the wall are not given
estimates.roof: cedar beams and planks (6:9). Drawn flat, as the text gives no pitch
estimates.partition: the inner sanctuary is 20 high (6:20) inside a house 30 high. It is drawn with a lower ceiling and an upper room above it (2 Chr 3:9 mentions upper rooms); some reconstructions raise its floor instead. The doorway is drawn 6 wide, as in Ezek 41:3, and 10 high
estimates.chains: 'across the front of the inner sanctuary' (6:21); drawn as two swags above its doorway. Their length and number are not given
estimates.cherubim: 10 high, of olive wood (6:23); the text gives no form. They stand on their feet facing the main room (2 Chr 3:13), so they are drawn as schematic standing figures
estimates.cherubim-wings: each wing is 5 cubits, and together the four span the room's 20, touching both walls and each other in the middle (6:24-27). Their height and shape are not given; they are drawn level at the shoulder
estimates.inner-doors: 'five-sided doorposts' (6:31) may instead mean a doorway a fifth of the wall's width. The doors are drawn standing open, since 8:8 says the ark's poles could be seen from the hall
estimates.doors: two doors of two folding leaves each (6:34), filling the 10-cubit doorway; drawn closed
estimates.veil: Chronicles has both a veil (3:14) and doors to the inner sanctuary (4:22) but does not say how they hung together. The veil is drawn just inside the doorway
estimates.court: 'three rows of dressed stone and one row of trimmed cedar beams' (6:36) is drawn as three courses a cubit high with cedar on top. The court's size is not given; it is drawn to leave room round the house for the altar, the Sea and the stands. Ezekiel's inner court is 100 cubits square (Ezek 40:47)
estimates.pillars: 18 high and 12 round (1 Kgs 7:15; Jer 52:21), so ≈3.8 across; Jeremiah adds that they were hollow, four fingers thick. 2 Chr 3:15 gives 35 cubits, often read as the two together. Whether they stood free or held up the porch roof is disputed. With 5-cubit capitals they come to 23, taller than the 20-cubit porch, so they are drawn standing free in front of it
estimates.capitals: 5 high (7:16; Jer 52:22). 2 Kgs 25:17 gives 3, perhaps not counting the lily-work. The form is inferred from 'bowl-shaped' (7:41) and 'shaped like lilies… four cubits' (7:19)
estimates.networks: lattice over each bowl and 'seven wreaths of chainwork' (7:17); the pattern is not given
estimates.pomegranates: two rows round each capital, 400 in all (7:42), so 100 a row. 2 Chr 3:16 gives a hundred; Jer 52:23 has 96 'on the sides' and 100 in all
estimates.sea: 10 across, 5 high and 30 round, a handbreadth thick with a lily-shaped brim (7:23-26). Measured across a circle 10 wide, the line should be ≈31.4, not 30. Drawn with the line round the body just below a brim that flares to the full 10, which is one common reading; another is that the 30 was measured inside the handbreadth-thick wall. The bowl's profile is not given. Drawn this way it holds ≈24.5 m³, about 1,100 baths of ≈22 litres. Kings says 2,000 baths and Chronicles 3,000, which would need a smaller bath or a fuller, more cylindrical vessel
estimates.sea-ornaments: two rows of gourds, ten to the cubit (7:24), so 300 a row round the 30-cubit line. Chronicles has 'figures of oxen' (2 Chr 4:3), probably from the similar Hebrew word for oxen (bakar) and gourds (peka'im)
estimates.oxen: their size is not given; drawn about life size, so the Sea stands 2.4 cubits off the ground. Schematic figures
estimates.stands: 4 × 4 × 3 (7:27). The 3 is taken to include the wheels. The supports and the handles (7:30, 34) are not drawn; each stand is corner uprights with the round band on top (7:35). Placed in a row on each side of the house (7:39); their spacing is not given
estimates.stand-panels: the panels between the uprights (7:28), drawn plain; their lions, oxen, cherubim and wreaths (7:29, 36) are not drawn
estimates.door-gold: 'gold hammered evenly over the carvings' (6:35) is drawn as a gold panel on each leaf
estimates.great-altar: Ahaz's altar, copied from one in Damascus (2 Kgs 16:10-11), is called 'the great altar' (16:15), but no size, material or form is given. It is drawn in stone, 14 × 14 × 7 cubits. It stands east of the bronze altar, which was 'between the new altar and the house' (16:14)
estimates.bronze-altar-north: the bronze altar moved 'to the north side of the new altar' (16:14), drawn without the ramp, which is itself an estimate
estimates.sea-on-stone: 'a stone base' (16:17) is the Hebrew for a pavement of stones. Drawn as a low platform a cubit high, since its size is not given
estimates.stand-wheels: a cubit and a half across (7:32), on axles, like chariot wheels (7:33); drawn as solid discs
estimates.basins: 4 cubits across, holding 40 baths (7:38). The depth is not given; a shallow bowl 1.4 cubits deep holds ≈900 litres, which is 40 baths of ≈22 litres. That depth is worked out from those figures, not stated
estimates.bronze-altar: 20 × 20 × 10 (2 Chr 4:1); drawn as a plain block with horns. The text does not say how priests reached a top 10 cubits up (Exod 20:26 forbids steps). A ramp is drawn on the south, 32 × 16 cubits, the size Mishnah Middot 3:3 gives for the Second Temple's altar. Placed on the axis in front of the porch; 2 Kgs 16:14 has it 'before the LORD… at the front of the temple'
estimates.incense-altar: shown as the tabernacle's (1 × 1 × 2, Exod 30:2); the size of Solomon's is not given
estimates.lampstands: each is shown as the tabernacle's lampstand; the text does not describe Solomon's beyond 'pure gold'. 'Five on the right side and five on the left' (7:49) is drawn as a row along each wall of the main hall, right being south
estimates.table: each table is shown as the tabernacle's (2 × 1 × 1½). Kings' one table is drawn in the middle of the north row, where the tabernacle's stood (Exod 26:35)
estimates.more-tables: Chronicles' ten (2 Chr 4:8), 'five on the south side and five on the north', are drawn in rows between the lampstands
estimates.ark: shown as the Ark of the covenant card builds it, beneath the middle of the cherubim's wings (8:6-7), its poles running east–west. 8:8 says the poles' ends could be seen from the Holy Place; the model's poles, ≈4½ cubits long, would not reach the doorway. b. Yoma 54a says they pressed out against the curtain 'like the two breasts of a woman'
